claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by a dynamic equilibrium between mechanical removal of a protective oxide film and rapid repassivation.
Mechanical stress intermittently disrupts the protective oxide film and exposes the underlying alloy to the electrolyte.
Abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative processes can contribute to wear in high-entropy alloys.
A surface oxide film can improve wear resistance by acting as a lubricant.
Optimal passive films are enriched in Cr, Mo, and Nb.
Compositions that facilitate rapid formation of a stable passive film minimize localized corrosion during ongoing wear.
The balance between oxide-film removal and kinetic repassivation reduces total material loss below the additive effects of independent wear and corrosion.
The specimens initially possess a stable passive oxide layer in the as-deposited and polished state.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl environment is sufficiently moderate to permit passive-film formation in the alloys under study.
Corrosion-event frequency and charge can be derived from electrochemical-noise measurements.
Higher charge per corrosion event indicates increased corrosion activity.
Rapidly repassivating alloys will show lower combined degradation than the arithmetic sum of independently measured wear and corrosion degradation.
Rapidly repassivating alloys will exhibit lower wear rates during combined tribocorrosion.
Rapidly repassivating alloys will exhibit smoother stabilization of the friction coefficient during combined tribocorrosion.
Rapidly repassivating alloys will exhibit reduced corrosion-event charge per cycle during combined tribocorrosion.
Matched specimens under solely mechanical or solely corrosive conditions lack rapid film recovery and therefore have higher net degradation.
The predicted benefit will fail when mechanical stress overwhelms repassivation capacity or when the electrolyte prevents passivation.
Quantitative repassivation-rate thresholds and the balance point between film removal and regrowth are unknown.
Combined degradation at or above the arithmetic sum of independent wear and corrosion, accompanied by no film recovery, would falsify the proposed enhanced-resistance mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes rapid film recovery to alloy composition, but the baseline assigns an absence of rapid recovery to compositionally matched specimens merely because they are tested under separate wear or corrosion conditions. Pure corrosion also does not impose the mechanical disruption that would inherently suppress film recovery.

The proposed falsifying observation of absent film recovery and additive-or-worse degradation can be reclassified as a boundary failure caused by overwhelming stress or an electrolyte that prevents passivation. Because no stress or repassivation threshold defines the valid domain, the stated observation is not unambiguously falsifying.
